Chapter 6: Spinors

6 Spinors

6.1 Lorentz and Spinors

Some Supplementary material for this section is Spinors for Beginners by Eigenchris which is very useful to get a grasp of the actual math that is going on.

6.1.1 Lorentz Transformations

Definition 6.1.1.1 (Metric Tensor).

A (or in special relativity, The) metric tensor is defined as being the dot product of basis vectors

𝑔𝜇𝜈=𝑒̂(𝜇)⋅𝑒̂(𝜈)

This definition is all but useless in Quantum Field Theory due to the whole theory entirely using Special Relativity instead of General Relativity1

The special relativity metric tensor (which is subject to arguments over convention), is either 𝑔𝜇𝜈=diag(+,−,−,−) or 𝑔𝜇𝜈=diag(−,+,+,+)2.

Definition 6.1.1.2 (Lorentz Transformation & Lorentz Invariance).

A Lorentz transformation Λ is defined as a coordinate transformation

Λ:(𝑡,𝑥,𝑦,𝑧)→(𝑡′,𝑥′,𝑦′,𝑧′)

such that

Λ𝑇𝑔Λ=𝑔

or

Λ𝛼𝜇Λ𝛽𝜈𝜂𝜇𝜈=𝜂𝛼𝛽

In special relativity (minkowski space), this condition is loosened to

𝑠2=𝑡2−𝑥2
is conserved but the previous condition is still useful in discussion of group theory and derivation of Spinors. Generally, Lorentz transformations are transformations that

6.1.2 Group Theory (cont’d)

Definition 6.1.2.1 (Lorentz Group).

This is the set of operations Λ such that

Λ𝑇𝑔Λ=𝑔

  • For instance, a Lorentz transformation could follow the 4-vector representation, defined as

    𝑥𝜇→Λ𝜇𝜈𝑥𝜈

  • More generally, a field 𝜙 transforms under a representation of the lorentz group as

    𝜙𝑖(𝑥)→𝑅(Λ)𝑖𝑗𝜙𝑗(Λ−1𝑥)

    (Similar to a matrix transformation)

  • The continuous Lorentz transformations that exist are rotations and boosts, which are the most general possible (continous) Lorentz transformations which can occur as they (+ the discrete Lorentz transformations such as 𝑃 and 𝑇) form the Lorentz Group

  • Rotations can be represented, again in the 4-vector representation, as rotation matrices. We let 𝜃𝑥,𝜃𝑦,𝜃𝑧 represent rotations in the 𝑥,𝑦,𝑧 axes respectively. Then, the rotation matrices can be represent as as

    Λ(𝜃𝑥)=(11cos𝜃𝑥sin𝜃𝑥−sin𝜃𝑥cos𝜃𝑥),Λ(𝜃𝑦)=(1cos𝜃𝑦−sin𝜃𝑦1sin𝜃𝑦cos𝜃𝑦)Λ(𝜃𝑧)=(1cos𝜃𝑧sin𝜃𝑧−sin𝜃𝑧cos𝜃𝑧1)

  • In a similar manner, boosts can be represented by matrices in the 4-vector representation. Denoting 𝛽𝑥,𝛽𝑦,𝛽𝑧 as the boost angles (in the hyperbolic trigonometric functions), we have that

    Λ(𝛽𝑥)=(cosh𝛽𝑥sinh𝛽𝑥sinh𝛽𝑥cosh𝛽𝑥11),Λ(𝛽𝑦)=(cosh𝛽𝑦sinh𝛽𝑦1sinh𝛽𝑦cosh𝛽𝑦1)Λ(𝛽𝑧)=(cosh𝛽𝑧sinh𝛽𝑧11sinh𝛽𝑧cosh𝛽𝑧)

  • Can utilize infinitesimal Lorentz transformations in order to extract the group (𝑂(1,3)) (we let 𝛽𝑖 parametrize boosts and 𝜃𝑖 parametrize rotations)

    • 𝛿𝑥0=𝛽𝑖𝑥𝑖𝛿𝑥𝑖=𝛽𝑖𝑥𝑜−𝜀𝑖𝑗𝑘𝜃𝑗𝑥𝑘

    or

    𝛿𝑥𝜇=𝑖[∑𝑖∈{1,2,3}𝜃(𝐽𝑖)𝜇𝜈+𝛽𝑖(𝐾𝑖)𝜇𝜈]𝑥𝜈
    • 𝐽𝑖 and 𝐾𝑖 matrices:
    𝐽1=𝑖(000−110),𝐽2=𝑖(0010−10),𝐽3=𝑖(00−1100)𝐾1=𝑖(0−1−1000),𝐾2=𝑖(0−10−100),𝐾3=𝑖(0−100−10)

    • Such matrices are generators of the Lorentz group

      • Can use to obtain the Lie Algebra
    • Λ=exp(𝑖𝜃𝑖𝐽𝑖+𝑖𝛽𝑖𝐾𝑖)

    6.2 Dirac Spinors (TODO)

    6.2.1 Spinors

    Definition 6.2.1.1 (Dirac Spinor).

    An object 𝜓 obeying the transormation properties

    𝜓→𝑆[Λ]𝜓,𝜓†→𝜓†𝑆[Λ]

  • What does this mean?

  • A lorentz transformation can be written as

    Λ𝜈𝜇=exp(12Ω𝜌𝜎(𝐽𝜌𝜎)𝜈𝜇)

    with new notation introduced for convenience such that Ω0𝑖=𝛽𝑖 boosts, Ω12=−Ω12=𝜃𝑧 (rotation angles) with (𝐽𝜌𝜎)𝜇𝜈=𝑔𝜌𝜇𝑔𝜎𝜈−𝑔𝜎𝜇𝑔𝜌𝜈

    • These are another way to write generators for the lorentz group

    • Notice that, using this tensor, we can write

      𝐾𝑖=−𝑖(𝐽0𝑖)𝜈𝜇

      for boosts and

      𝐽𝑖=𝑖2𝜀𝑖𝑗𝑘(𝐽𝑗𝑘)𝜈𝜇
      for rotations

  • These generators form 𝔰𝔬(1,3), the Lorentz Algebra

    • Their exponential gives a representation of the Lorentz Group double cover Spin(1,3)≅SL(2,ℂ)

Theorem 6.2.1.2.

The Lorentz Algebra, 𝔰𝔬(1,3), has two commuting sub-algebras represented by the 3d rotation algebras 𝔰𝔲(2)

Proof.

  • Notice that if we switch back to 𝐽𝑖 and 𝐾𝑖, we can derive SU(2), the group for spinors.

  • Define 𝐽𝑖+≡12(𝐽𝑖+𝑖𝐾𝑖), 𝐽𝑖−≡12(𝐽𝑖−𝑖𝐾𝑖)

  • We have then,

    [𝐽𝑖+,𝐽𝑗+]=𝑖𝜀𝑖𝑗𝑘𝐽𝑘+[𝐽𝑖−,𝐽𝑗−]=𝑖𝜀𝑖𝑗𝑘𝐽𝑘−[𝐽𝑖+,𝐽𝑖−]=0

    hence, 𝔰𝔬(1,3) has 2 communiting sub algebras, both of which are 3d rotation groups given by the Levi-Cevita connections. Hence, SO(1,3)≅SU(2)⊕SU(2)

⁠□

  • Hence, we now have the definition of a spinor

Definition 6.2.1.3 (Spinor).

A Spinor is an object that transforms under SU(2)

6.2.2 Clifford Algebruh

  • To construct Dirac Spinors, one must first construct gamma matrices, which form the basis of a Clifford Algebra 𝒞︁𝓁︁1,3(ℝ)

Definition 6.2.2.1 (Gamma Matrices).

Gamma matrices are defined as being anticommuting matrices such that

{𝛾𝜇,𝛾𝜈}=2𝑔𝜇𝜈

and having the property that

(𝛾0)2=1,(𝛾𝑖)2=−1

  • As seen in the math toolkit, these matrices can be represented as

    𝛾𝜇=(𝜎𝜇𝜎̄𝜇)

    with 𝜎𝜇=(𝟙,𝜎⃗),𝜎̄𝜇=(𝟙,−𝜎⃗) and 𝜎𝑖 being Pauli Matrices

    • This representation is known as the Weyl Representation
  • An additional piece of useful notation is the idea that 𝑝=𝑝𝜇𝛾𝜇=𝑝𝜇𝛾𝜇

6.2.3 Pauli Matrix and Gamma Matrix Indentities

𝜎𝑖𝜎𝑗=𝛿𝑖𝑗𝑖𝜀𝑖𝑗𝑘𝜎𝑘,{𝜎𝑖,𝜎𝑗}=2𝛿𝑖𝑗,[𝜎𝑖,𝜎𝑗]=2𝑖𝜀𝑖𝑗𝑘𝜎𝑘

For Pauli Matrices

  • A useful quantity to define is a representation of the Lorentz Algebra

    𝑆𝜌𝜎=12[𝛾𝜌,𝛾𝜎]=12𝛾𝜌𝛾𝜎−12𝑔𝜌𝜎

6.2.4 Lorentz Group Representation

  • We now want to derive why spinors behave the way that they do. That is, why do they have spin 12?

  • As seen before, we have our generators written as linear combinations

    𝐽𝑖+≡12(𝐽𝑖+𝑖𝐾𝑖),𝐽𝑖−≡12(𝐽𝑖−𝑖𝐾𝑖)

    which formed two commuting subgroups SO(1,3)≅SU(2)×SU(2)

  • There are rotation generators 𝐽⃗ and hence the Lorentz group is a super of SO(3)

    • Any representation of SO(3) is a representation of the Lorentz Group

  • Notice that SU(2) both have quantum numbers 𝐴 and 𝐵. The spin is their sum.

𝔰𝔲(2)⊕𝔰𝔲(2) representation(𝐴,𝐵)(0,0)(12,0)(0,12)(12,12)(1,1)
𝔰𝔬(3) representation𝑗=𝐴+𝐵012121⊕02⊕1⊕0

  • In this table, you can see that there are two different representations of 𝑗=12. Therefore, there are two different type of spinors (this corresponds to chirality which you will see)

  • Now we 2×2 matrices such that

    [𝐽𝑖+,𝐽𝑗+]=𝑖𝜖𝑖𝑗𝑘𝐽𝑘+[𝐽𝑖−,𝐽𝑗−]=𝑖𝜖𝑖𝑗𝑘𝐽𝑘−[𝐽𝑖+,𝐽𝑗−]=0

  • Remember our sigma matrix identities?, we had that

    [𝜎𝑖2,𝜎𝑗2]=𝑖𝜀𝑖𝑗𝑘𝜎𝑘2

    which is the perfect 𝔰𝔬(3) algebra that we wanted

    • For the (12,0) representation, we can set 𝐽+=0 and 𝐽𝑖−=12𝜎𝑖 as our generators
    • For the (0,12) representation, we can set 𝐽−=0 and 𝐽𝑖+=12𝜎𝑖 as our generators

  • Now we are able to get our Lorentz transformations.

    • For rotations 𝐽⃗=𝐽⃗−+𝐽⃗+
    • For our boosts, 𝐾⃗=𝑖(𝐽⃗−−𝐽⃗+)

  • Thus,

    (12,0):𝐽⃗=12𝜎⃗,𝐾⃗=𝑖2𝜎⃗(0,12):𝐽⃗=12𝜎⃗,𝐾⃗=−𝑖2𝜎⃗

6.2.5 Note: Hermicity

  • Rotations are hermitian and boosts are anti hermitian

  • Now we have an even better way to define spinors in terms of their handedness

Definition 6.2.5.1 (Right Handed Weyl Spinor).

  • An object transforming under the (0,12) representation of the Lorentz group

  • Right handed weyl spinors transform as

    𝜓𝑅→𝑒12(𝑖𝜃𝑗𝜎𝑗+𝛽𝑗𝜎𝑗)𝜓𝑅=(1+𝑖2𝜃𝑗𝜎𝑗+12𝛽𝑗𝜎𝑗+…)𝜓𝑅

Definition 6.2.5.2 (Left Handed Weyl Spinor).

  • An object transforming under the (12,0) representation of the Lorentz group

  • These transform as

    𝜓𝐿→𝑒12(𝑖𝜃𝑗𝜎𝑗−𝛽𝑗𝜎𝑗)𝜓𝐿=(1+𝑖2𝜃𝑗𝜎𝑗−12𝛽𝑗𝜎𝑗+…)𝜓𝐿

  • There are also infinitesimal transformations which are

    𝛿𝜓𝑅=12(𝑖𝜃𝑗+𝛽𝑗)𝜎𝑗𝜓𝑅𝛿𝜓𝐿=12(𝑖𝜃𝑗−𝛽𝑗)𝜎𝑗𝜓𝐿𝛿𝜓𝑅†=12(−𝑖𝜃𝑗+𝛽𝑗)𝜓𝑅†𝜎𝑗𝛿𝜓𝐿†=12(−𝑖𝜃𝑗−𝛽𝑗)𝜓𝐿†𝜎𝑗

6.2.6 note: Unitarity

Since there is no finite dimensional unitary representation of the lorentz group, spinor bases must be built in terms of momentum, much like the photon field

6.2.7 Lorentz Invariant Lagrangian

  • How do we get a Lorentz invariant lagrangian with our new spinor valued fields?

  • First, let us write

    • (12,0) rep:

      𝜓𝑅(𝑥)=(𝜓1𝑅(𝑥)𝜓2𝑅(𝑥))

    • (0,12) rep:

      𝜓(𝑥)=(𝜓1𝐿(𝑥)𝜓2𝐿(𝑥))

  • We want a lagrangian with the right number of DOF, of course

  • Let us be naive and write

    ℒ︀=(𝜓𝑅)†☐𝜓𝑅+𝑚2(𝜓𝑅)†𝜓𝑅

    • not L.I.:

      𝛿(𝜓𝑅†𝜓𝑅)=12𝜓𝑅†[𝑖𝜃𝑗+𝛽𝑗𝜎𝑗𝜓𝑅]+12[𝜓𝑅†(−𝑖𝜃𝑗+𝛽𝑗)𝜎𝑗]𝜓𝑅=𝛽𝑖𝜓𝑝†𝜎𝑖𝜓𝑅≠0

  • Therefore, we must have two fields 𝜓𝑅 and 𝜓𝐿

    • Let’s try terms like 𝜓𝐿†𝜓𝑅:

      𝛿(𝜓𝐿†𝜓𝑅)=[𝜓𝐿†𝑖2(−𝑖𝜃𝑖−𝛽𝑖)𝜎𝑖]𝜓𝑅+𝜓𝐿†[𝑖2(𝑖𝜃𝑖+𝛽𝑖)𝜎𝑖𝜓𝑅]=0

    • Adding the h.c. will give us a lagrangian:

      ℒ︀Dirac Mass=𝑚(𝜓𝐿†𝜓𝑅+𝜓𝑅†𝜓𝐿)

  • Now we want kinetic terms to add to the lagrangian

    • we can try adding terms like ℒ︀kin=𝜓𝐿†□𝜓𝑅+𝜓𝑅†□𝜓𝐿 but these are “not interesting”

    • Let’s look at a term like 𝜓𝑅†𝜎𝑖𝜓𝑅: [

      𝛿(𝜓𝑅†𝜎𝑖𝜓𝑅)=12𝜓𝑅†𝜎𝑖[(𝑖𝜃𝑗+𝛽𝑗)𝜎𝑗𝜓𝑅]+12[𝜓𝑅†(−𝑖𝜃𝑗+𝛽𝑗)𝜎𝑗]𝜎𝑖𝜓𝑅=𝛽𝑗2𝜓𝑅†(𝜎𝑖𝜎𝑗+𝜎𝑗𝜎𝑖)𝜓𝑅+𝑖𝜃𝑗2(𝜎𝑖𝜎𝑗−𝜎𝑗𝜎𝑖)𝜓𝑅=𝛽𝑖𝜓𝑅†𝜓𝑅−𝜃𝑗𝜖𝑖𝑗𝑘𝜓𝑅†𝜎𝑘𝜓𝑅

      ]

      ∴𝛿(𝜓𝑅†𝜓𝑅,𝜓𝑅†𝜎𝑖𝜓𝑅)=(𝛽𝑖𝜓𝑅†𝜎𝑖𝜓𝑅,𝛽𝑖𝜓𝑅†𝜓𝑅−𝜖𝑖𝑗𝑘𝐵𝑗𝜓𝑅†𝜎𝑘𝜓𝑅)

  • Notice that this is exactly how a vector transforms

    • 𝛿(𝑣0,𝑣𝑖)=(𝛽𝑖𝑣𝑖,𝛽𝑖𝑣0−𝜖𝑖𝑗𝑘𝜃𝑗𝑣𝑘)
